questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis for 10 days. The ulcer has a clean base, indurated edges, and is associated with unilateral non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Dark-field microscopy of the ulcer exudate shows motile spiral organisms. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
questions.exp: The presentation is classic primary syphilis (Hunterian chancre) caused by Treponema pallidum. Dark-field microscopy showing motile spirochetes confirms the diagnosis. Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose is the treatment of choice for primary syphilis per WHO/CDC guidelines.

questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a chronic ulcer on the dorsum of the foot with sinus tracts discharging granules. The granules are yellow-white. Microscopy shows branching filaments. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.exp: Yellow-white granules in mycetoma suggest Actinomadura madurae (actinomycetoma). Black granules suggest Madurella mycetomatis (eumycetoma). Actinomycetoma shows branching filaments (bacteria) on microscopy and is treated with co-trimoxazole + amikacin, while eumycetoma requires antifungals.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with erythematous plaques over the malar area and bridge of nose, sparing the nasolabial folds, along with discoid lesions on the scalp and photosensitivity. ANA is positive at 1:320 with anti-dsDNA antibodies positive. Which of the following skin findings is MOST specific for SLE?
questions.exp: While malar rash is characteristic of SLE, discoid lupus lesions (scarring plaques causing permanent alopecia and dyspigmentation) are more specific for lupus erythematosus overall and can occur in SLE. Anti-dsDNA antibodies confirm SLE. Periungual telangiectasia is more typical of dermatomyositis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man develops tense bullae on the trunk and extremities with no mucosal involvement. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposits along the basement membrane zone. ELISA is positive for anti-BP180 antibodies. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid typically affects elderly patients with tense bullae, no mucosal involvement, eosinophilia, linear IgG/C3 along BMZ on DIF, and antibodies against BP180 (type XVII collagen) and BP230. Pemphigus shows intraepidermal split with IgG/C3 in chicken-wire pattern.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presented with hypopigmented macules and patches on the trunk and arms with loss of sensation. Slit skin smear shows 2+ bacillary index. Histopathology shows foamy macrophages containing acid-fast bacilli with no granuloma formation. What type of leprosy is this?
questions.exp: Lepromatous leprosy (LL) presents with multiple, poorly defined, hypopigmented macules with reduced sensation. Histology shows foamy macrophages (Virchow cells) containing M. leprae with no granuloma formation (absent cell-mediated immunity). BI is high (4–6+). TB leprosy shows well-formed granulomas with few/no bacilli.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth that started as vesicles. Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which of the following is the treatment of choice for localized disease?
questions.exp: Non-bullous impetigo caused by S. aureus or S. pyogenes presents with honey-coloured crusts. For localized disease without systemic features, topical mupirocin 2% (or retapamulin) is the first-line treatment. Oral antibiotics are reserved for extensive disease, bullous impetigo, or systemic signs.

questions.q: A 55-year-old immunosuppressed patient develops grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the right T6 dermatome, associated with severe pain. He develops new vesicles 5 days after onset. Which antiviral drug should be initiated?
opts: Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days
Any of the above are appropriate
questions.exp: Herpes zoster in an immunosuppressed patient requires antiviral therapy ideally within 72 hours of rash onset. Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times daily for 7 days, valacyclovir 1000 mg TDS for 7 days, and famciclovir 500 mg TDS for 7 days are all acceptable. Valacyclovir and famciclovir have better oral bioavailability.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with scaly erythematous plaques over elbows, knees, and scalp with nail pitting and oil spots. Auspitz sign is positive. Histopathology shows parakeratosis, suprapapillary thinning, and Munro microabscesses. What is the pathological hallmark in the dermis?
opts: Dilated tortuous capillaries in dermal papillae
questions.exp: The pathological hallmark of psoriasis in the dermis is dilated and tortuous capillaries in elongated dermal papillae with thin suprapapillary plates, explaining the Auspitz sign. Munro microabscesses (neutrophils in stratum corneum) and Kogoj spongiform pustules (subcorneal neutrophilic collections) are epidermal changes.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents with a slowly enlarging pearly nodule on the nose with central umbilication and rolled telangiectatic borders. The lesion has been present for 2 years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common skin malignancy and typically presents as a slow-growing pearly nodule with rolled, translucent borders and central telangiectasia on sun-exposed areas (commonly the nose). It arises from basal keratinocytes. Keratoacanthoma grows rapidly over weeks.

questions.q: A patient with leprosy on standard MDT develops sudden onset of painful, erythematous, tender nodules on the extensor aspects of limbs, associated with fever and joint pains. Histopathology of the nodule shows panniculitis with neutrophilic infiltrate. What is this reaction?
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL/Type 2 reaction) occurs in LL and BL leprosy, presenting with tender erythematous nodules, fever, joint pains, and systemic features. It is an immune complex-mediated (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction. Treatment is thalidomide or prednisolone. Type 1 reaction shows upgrading of existing lesions.

questions.q: A 32-year-old HIV-positive man presents with multiple painless ulcers over the genitalia, perineum, and thighs. The ulcers have a beefy-red granulomatous base with raised, rolled borders. Tissue smear shows intracellular Donovan bodies within large mononuclear cells. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Doxycycline 100 mg BD for minimum 3 weeks
questions.exp: Donovanosis (granuloma inguinale) is caused by Klebsiella granulomatis. Donovan bodies (bipolar staining intracellular organisms in macrophages) on smear are pathognomonic. Doxycycline 100 mg BD for minimum 3 weeks (until all lesions have healed) is the first-line treatment. Azithromycin 1g weekly is an alternative.

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl presents with multiple comedones, papules, and pustules over the face, chest, and back. She has not responded to topical benzoyl peroxide and topical adapalene for 3 months. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.exp: For moderate acne unresponsive to topical therapy, the next step is oral antibiotics (doxycycline/minocycline) combined with topical retinoid (adapalene/tretinoin) and/or benzoyl peroxide. Oral isotretinoin is reserved for severe nodulo-cystic acne, scarring acne, or failure of 2 courses of oral antibiotics. Antibiotic monotherapy should be avoided.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman on hydroxychloroquine for SLE presents with progressive visual field defects. Ophthalmologic examination reveals a 'bull's eye' maculopathy. What mechanism underlies this toxicity?
opts: Deposition of drug in retinal pigment epithelium causing photoreceptor damage
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine retinopathy results from drug accumulation in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), causing irreversible photoreceptor damage leading to the characteristic 'bull's eye' maculopathy. Annual ophthalmologic screening is mandatory after 5 years or earlier in high-risk patients. Maximum dose should not exceed 5 mg/kg/day.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with multiple flesh-coloured warty papules over the perianal area. He reports receptive anal intercourse. HPV typing reveals HPV 16. What is the significance of this finding?
opts: Low oncogenic potential; treat with topical podophyllin
High oncogenic potential; requires biopsy and close follow-up for anal intraepithelial neoplasia
questions.exp: HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk (high oncogenic potential) strains associated with anogenital cancers and intraepithelial neoplasia. HPV 16 is the most common high-risk type found in anal and cervical cancers. Condyloma acuminata is typically caused by HPV 6 and 11 (low-risk). Biopsy to rule out AIN and close surveillance is essential.

questions.q: During patch testing, a patient develops an erythematous vesicular reaction at the site of nickel sulfate application at 48 and 96 hours. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is responsible for this?
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis and patch test reactions are classic examples of Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity, mediated by sensitized T lymphocytes (CD4+ Th1 cells and CD8+ cytotoxic T cells). The reaction peaks at 48–96 hours after allergen contact. Patch testing is the gold standard for diagnosing allergic contact dermatitis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive thickening of the skin of the face and hands, difficulty opening the mouth, and Raynaud's phenomenon for 2 years. ANA is positive with anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) antibody. What pattern of systemic sclerosis is she most likely to have?
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) antibody is associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) and carries a higher risk of interstitial lung disease and worse prognosis. lcSSc is associated with anti-centromere antibody and CREST syndrome. dcSSc involves trunk and proximal extremities in addition to face and distal extremities.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a rapidly growing nodule on the shin that ulcerates. Histopathology shows sheets of large atypical cells with abundant pale cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei, and frequent mitoses; cells stain positive for CK20 and CD56, negative for CK7. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Merkel cell carcinoma (primary neuroendocrine carcinoma of skin) presents as a rapidly growing, firm, reddish-violaceous nodule in elderly/immunosuppressed patients. CK20 positivity in a paranuclear dot pattern combined with CD56, synaptophysin, and chromogranin positivity, with CK7 negativity, is pathognomonic. Associated with Merkel cell polyomavirus.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with shallow, painful oral ulcers and flaccid bullae over the trunk and face that rupture easily leaving raw erosions. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF shows IgG deposits in an intercellular 'fish-net' pattern throughout the epidermis. Which antigen is targeted?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) presents with mucocutaneous flaccid bullae and erosions with positive Nikolsky sign. DIF shows IgG in intercellular spaces (chicken-wire pattern). PV targets desmoglein 3 (mucosal type), while pemphigus foliaceus targets desmoglein 1 (skin type). The mucosal involvement in PV indicates desmoglein 3 antibodies.

questions.q: A newborn presents with blistering at sites of minor trauma from birth. Blisters heal without scarring. EM shows cleavage at the level of the lamina lucida. Immunofluorescence mapping with anti-laminin 5 shows absent staining. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Junctional EB (JEB) shows cleavage within the lamina lucida of the basement membrane zone. The Herlitz subtype (most severe) has absent laminin 332 (laminin 5) staining. JEB shows blistering without milia formation (in contrast to dystrophic EB which heals with scarring and milia). EB simplex shows intraepidermal split (basal keratinocyte level).

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. He also has pathergy test positivity. HLA-B51 is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Behcet disease is characterized by the triad of recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and ocular involvement (uveitis). Pathergy test positivity (papule/pustule at site of needlestick) and HLA-B51 association are characteristic. It is a systemic vasculitis common in the 'Silk Road' countries including India and Turkey.

questions.q: A 30-year-old dark-skinned woman develops bilateral symmetrical hyperpigmented patches over the cheeks, forehead, and upper lip that worsen in summer. She is on oral contraceptives. Which of the following is the MOST effective treatment combination?
opts: Triple combination cream (hydroquinone 4% + tretinoin 0.05% + fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%) with strict photoprotection
questions.exp: Melasma management requires strict sun protection (SPF 30+, broad-spectrum) as the foundation. The Kligman's modified triple combination cream (hydroquinone 4% + tretinoin 0.05% + fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%) is the most effective first-line topical treatment as per evidence. OCP-induced melasma may improve after switching contraceptives.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs a Tzanck smear from the base of a fresh vesicle in a patient with genital herpes. What is the characteristic finding?
opts: Multinucleated giant cells (acantholytic cells) with ground-glass nuclei
questions.exp: Tzanck smear in herpes simplex/zoster infections shows multinucleated giant cells (Tzanck cells) with ground-glass (ballooned) nuclei and nuclear molding — this is the characteristic finding. Henderson-Paterson bodies (molluscum bodies) are seen in molluscum contagiosum. Tzanck smear cannot differentiate HSV from VZV.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man presents with scaling, erythema, and hair loss in a circular patch on the scalp. KOH mount shows hair shafts packed with small arthroconidia inside the hair shaft. Wood's lamp examination shows dull green fluorescence. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Endothrix tinea capitis (arthroconidia inside the hair shaft) with Wood's lamp fluorescence is seen with Microsporum species. Microsporum audouinii causes epidemic tinea capitis in children with yellow-green fluorescence on Wood's lamp and endothrix pattern. T. tonsurans causes endothrix but NO fluorescence. M. canis (from cats) also fluoresces.

questions.q: A 65-year-old woman on long-term methotrexate for psoriasis develops nausea, oral ulcers, and thrombocytopenia. Which supplement should have been co-prescribed to prevent mucosal and haematological toxicity?
opts: Folic acid 5 mg daily (except on methotrexate days)
questions.exp: Methotrexate is a folate antagonist; folic acid 5 mg daily (given on all days except the methotrexate day) significantly reduces mucositis, GI upset, hepatotoxicity, and haematological toxicity without reducing efficacy. Folinic acid (leucovorin) is used to rescue from methotrexate toxicity in overdose situations.

questions.q: A 40-year-old man undergoes surgical excision of a pigmented lesion on the back. Histopathology shows atypical melanocytes at the dermoepidermal junction arranged in single cells and nests, with upward pagetoid spread and marked cytological atypia. The lesion is confined to the epidermis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Melanoma in situ (superficial spreading type) shows atypical melanocytes confined to the epidermis with prominent pagetoid spread (upward migration of atypical cells) arranged in nests and single units at the DEJ. Lentigo maligna type occurs on sun-damaged skin (face) with lentiginous pattern in elderly. Dysplastic naevus shows architectural disorder but less severe atypia.

questions.q: A 55-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with well-defined erythema, hyperpigmentation, and scaling in sun-exposed areas (dorsum of hands, V of neck, forehead). He also has diarrhoea and dementia. What is the underlying deficiency?
questions.exp: Pellagra results from niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency, presenting with the classic '4Ds': Dermatitis (photosensitive, symmetrical on sun-exposed areas), Diarrhoea, Dementia, and Death. Casal's necklace describes the collar-like distribution around the neck. It is common in maize-eating populations and chronic alcoholics. Treated with nicotinamide.

questions.q: A 29-year-old woman presents with annular erythematous scaly plaques with central clearing on the inner thighs and groin. KOH shows septate hyphae. Which topical antifungal is LEAST likely to be effective due to increasing resistance?
questions.exp: Tinea cruris in India is predominantly caused by Trichophyton mentagrophytes complex (now T. indotineae) which shows increasing resistance to azoles (including clotrimazole, fluconazole, itraconazole) due to ergosterol biosynthesis gene mutations (ERG11). T. indotineae (a hypervirulent strain) remains sensitive to terbinafine and other allylamines.

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman presents with tightened facial skin, loss of normal skin folds, telangiectasia, and mat-like deposits visible over the face (calcinosis). She has GERD and Raynaud's phenomenon for 10 years before skin tightening. What antibody is characteristic of her condition?
questions.exp: CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia) is a variant of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc) associated with anti-centromere antibody (ACA). Raynaud's phenomenon preceding skin disease by years is typical of lcSSc. Anti-Scl-70 is associated with dcSSc with ILD.

questions.q: While performing liquid nitrogen cryotherapy for a plantar wart, the dermatologist applies the probe for 30 seconds achieving a freeze ball extending 2 mm beyond the wart margin. A blister forms the next day. What temperature is achieved at the lesion site during cryotherapy?
questions.exp: Liquid nitrogen boils at -196°C, but the temperature at the tissue-probe interface during clinical cryotherapy reaches approximately -20°C to -50°C (typically -25°C is cited for tissue destruction). A freeze ball of 2-3 mm beyond the lesion margin is adequate for warts. The critical temperature for cell death is -20°C to -30°C at the lesion margin.

questions.q: A 38-year-old male with no prior history presents with erythema, edema, and vesiculation of both hands after starting a new job as a dishwasher. The reaction is worst on the web spaces and dorsa of hands. Which of the following best distinguishes allergic contact dermatitis from irritant contact dermatitis?
opts: Allergic contact dermatitis requires a sensitization period before reaction
Irritant contact dermatitis can spread beyond the area of contact (id reaction)
Allergic contact dermatitis occurs with first exposure at any concentration
Irritant contact dermatitis requires patch testing to confirm
questions.exp: Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is a Type IV hypersensitivity that requires a sensitization period (typically 10–14 days for primary sensitization) before reaction on re-exposure. ACD can spread beyond the contact site. Irritant contact dermatitis (ICD) occurs with first exposure at sufficient concentration without prior sensitization and is dose-dependent. Patch testing confirms ACD.

questions.q: A 48-year-old male presents with multiple satellite papules surrounding a primary nodule on the nose, with similar lesions along the lymphatic drainage. He is an immunocompromised patient with history of gardening injury. Culture at 25°C shows branching hyphae; at 37°C shows yeast-like cells. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Sporotrichosis caused by Sporothrix schenckii presents as lymphocutaneous spread from a primary inoculation site (sporotrichoid spread). The dimorphic fungus grows as hyphae at 25°C and yeast at 37°C. Oral itraconazole 200 mg daily for 3–6 months is the first-line treatment. SSKI is an older alternative. Amphotericin B is for severe/disseminated disease.
